decks.name: LeetCode #286 - Walls and Gates (Islands and Treasure)
decks.description: Fill each empty room with distance to its nearest gate (treasure) in a 2D grid

cards.question: Walls and Gates (Islands and Treasure): You are given an m x n 2D grid initialized with three possible values: -1 represents a wall or obstacle, 0 represents a gate (treasure), and INF (2147483647) represents an empty room. Fill each empty room with the distance to its nearest gate. If it is impossible to reach a gate, leave it as INF. You may assume the grid will only contain -1, 0, or INF.

solutions.name: Brute Force (Backtracking)
solutions.explanation: Use DFS with backtracking to explore all paths from each empty room to find nearest treasure. For each INF cell, perform DFS that explores all four directions. DFS returns INF if out of bounds, wall, or already visited in current path. Returns 0 if treasure found. Otherwise, mark cell as visited, recursively try all directions taking minimum distance, unmark cell (backtrack), and return result plus 1. This explores all possible paths to find minimum distance. Very inefficient as it explores exponential paths. Time O(m*n*4^(m*n)) in worst case due to exploring all paths. Space O(m*n) for visited array and recursion stack.

solutions.timeDescription: For each of m*n cells with INF, we explore all possible paths which can branch into 4 directions at each step, leading to exponential time in worst case
solutions.spaceDescription: Visited array requires O(m*n) space. Recursion stack depth can go up to m*n in worst case of exploring entire grid
solutions.exampleWalkthrough: Given grid [[INF,-1,0,INF],[INF,INF,INF,-1],[INF,-1,INF,-1],[0,-1,INF,INF]]: For cell (0,0) with INF, DFS explores all paths. Try going down: visits (1,0), (2,0), reaches (3,0) with treasure at distance 3. Try going right path: hits wall at (0,1). Backtracking allows exploring multiple paths. After trying all paths from (0,0), minimum distance is 3. Repeat for all INF cells. Very slow due to exploring all possible paths.

solutions.name: Breadth First Search
solutions.explanation: Use BFS from each empty room to find its nearest treasure. For each INF cell, perform BFS exploring cells level by level. Start with current cell in queue and visited set. Process queue level by level, tracking steps. For each cell dequeued, check if it's treasure (return steps). Otherwise, add valid unvisited neighbors to queue. Increment steps after each level. If queue empties without finding treasure, return INF. This finds shortest path from each empty room to nearest treasure. More efficient than backtracking but still repeats work. Time O((m*n)^2) as we do BFS from each of m*n empty rooms, each BFS visiting up to m*n cells. Space O(m*n) for queue and visited set.

solutions.timeDescription: For each of potentially m*n empty rooms, we perform BFS that can visit up to m*n cells in worst case, resulting in quadratic time complexity
solutions.spaceDescription: Each BFS uses visited array of size m*n and queue that can store up to m*n cells in worst case
solutions.exampleWalkthrough: Given grid [[INF,-1,0,INF],[INF,INF,INF,-1],[INF,-1,INF,-1],[0,-1,INF,INF]]: For cell (0,0) with INF, BFS starts at (0,0). Level 0: check (0,0), not treasure. Level 1: add (1,0). Level 2: from (1,0) add (2,0). Level 3: from (2,0) add (3,0), found treasure, return 3. Set grid[0][0]=3. Repeat BFS for cell (0,3): BFS explores right column finding treasure at distance 4. Continue for all INF cells. More efficient than backtracking but still does redundant work.

solutions.name: Multi-Source BFS
solutions.explanation: Use multi-source BFS starting from all treasures simultaneously. Instead of BFS from each empty room, start BFS from all treasures at once. Initialize queue with all treasure positions (cells with value 0). Process queue level by level, for each cell, set distance and add valid unvisited neighbors. Helper function addCell checks bounds, visited status, and walls before adding to queue. This way, treasures expand outward like ripples, naturally filling each empty room with distance to nearest treasure. Each cell visited exactly once. Much more efficient than previous approaches. Time O(m*n) as each cell added to queue once. Space O(m*n) for queue and visited set.

solutions.timeDescription: Each cell is added to queue at most once and processed once. We visit all cells in the grid exactly once during the multi-source BFS
solutions.spaceDescription: Queue can hold up to m*n cells in worst case. Visited set stores up to m*n coordinates
solutions.exampleWalkthrough: Given grid [[INF,-1,0,INF],[INF,INF,INF,-1],[INF,-1,INF,-1],[0,-1,INF,INF]]: Initialize queue with treasures at (0,2) and (3,0), mark as visited. Distance 0: set grid[0][2]=0 and grid[3][0]=0, add neighbors (0,3) and (2,0). Distance 1: process (0,3) and (2,0), set values to 1, add their neighbors (1,3) and (1,0). Distance 2: process (1,3) and (1,0), set values to 2, add neighbors. Continue until all reachable cells filled. Result: [[3,-1,0,1],[2,2,1,-1],[1,-1,2,-1],[0,-1,3,4]].
